Dragonfly 3D World Licenses
Licenses define the rights to use Dragonfly 3D World on designated equipment at a certain level of functionality. In addition, licenses can be perpetual or may be restricted to a specific period of time. For example, annual and monthly subscriptions for Dragonfly are only valid until a given data. Each time the software runs, it checks for a valid license. If a valid license is found, the application will run with all of the licensed features.
The currently licensed features are listed in the License box in the About dialog, as shown below. Choose Help > About Dragonfly to open the About dialog.
Company and License boxes
Questions about licensing should be addressed to our Sales Team (sales.dragonfly@comet.tech).
The following table summarizes the optional features that can be separately licensed for Dragonfly 3D World commercial use.
Licensing options
Item
Description
Bone Analysis
Is a pre-clinical research application designed for the evaluation of high-resolution micro-CT images of bone specimens.
Deep Learning
Includes the Deep Learning Tool training deep models for image segmentation and regression tasks and the Segmentation Wizard, which provides an easy-to-use, guided workflow for implementing deep learning and classical machine learning segmentation of multi-dimensional images.
Plug Analysis
Provides a dedicated workflow for analyzing core plugs acquired from rock samples and other porous media.
Remote Access
Lets you work anywhere, at any time — at the microscope, in your office, or even in the coffee shop. The remote access add-in provides advanced 3D visualization and analysis throughout your institution's network and from remote locations.

documents.title: Generating Dragonfly VS Code Workspaces
documents.text:
Generating Dragonfly VS Code Workspaces
You can set up a complete development environment for working with Dragonfly using Visual Studio (VS) Code and Roo AI as your intelligent coding assistant. This helps bridge the gap between Dragonfly's powerful imaging platform and modern AI-assisted development. Roo understands Dragonfly's code base and can help with code completion and suggestions, debugging, code refactoring, and documentation generation to accelerate plug-in development and modification, custom tool creation, and integration tasks.
Generated VS code workspace files (*.code-workspace extension) include:
Python source code directories (user extensions, core Python modules).
Proper Python interpreter configuration pointing to Dragonfly's embedded Python environment.
Pre-configured folder structure for efficient navigation.
Recommendations and help installing of essential extensions, including Roo-Cline extension, Python development tools (IntelliSense, debugging, linting and so on).
Checks for required tools, including Visual Studio Core and UV package manager for Python dependency management, as well as guidance if tools are missing.
Detailed instructions for installing the required packages and saving a Dragonfly VS code workspace are available at: https://dev.theobjects.com/dragonfly_2025_1_release/Documentation/SetupForDevelopmentWithVSCode/setupfordevelopmentwithvscode.html.

documents.title: GPGPU Acceleration
documents.text:
GPGPU Acceleration
Dragonfly's GPGPU (general-purpose computing on graphics processing units) framework provides significantly faster processing times for image filtering, skeletonization, segmentation, mesh generation, and other compute-intensive tasks than CPU-based image processing. Supported hardware on Windows and Linux includes AMD and NVIDIA GPUs, as well as Intel ARC GPUs and Intel integrated graphics UHD that support OpenGL 4.3 and up.
In most cases, GPGPU acceleration out performs CPU-based image processing by leveraging the parallel processing power of GPUs. GPUs have thousands of small processing cores that can execute the same instruction on multiple pixels simultaneously, which makes them highly efficient, especially for large images or complex algorithms.
As shown in the graph below, processing times on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs, as well as on Intel integrated graphics UHD, can experience multiple orders of magnitude improvement in performance compared to processing on CPU while maintaining accuracy and precision.
Comparative benchmark of GPU versus CPU processing of a USHORT 1024×1024×1024 dataset
Not all GPUs are equally suited for image processing. Selecting the appropriate hardware is crucial for achieving optimal performance.
GPGPU Preferences
You must select the Miscellaneous preference 'Use GPGPU acceleration (when available)', as shown below, to run applicable operations with GPGPU acceleration. If not selected, the CPU equivalent will be used.
Miscellaneous preferences
GPGPU Accelerated Image Filters
The following image filters have been integrated within the GPGPU framework.
In most cases, you should not notice any differences between the image filtering outputs of GPGPU versus CPU processing. You can verify this by comparing the structural similarity index (SSIM) of the GPGPU and CPU outputs in Dragonfly’s Processed Image Comparator (see Processed Image Comparator).
Available GPGPU operations for image filtering
Filter
Description
Bilateral
This smoothing filter preserves edges and reduces noise by averaging pixels based
on their spatial closeness and radiometric similarity.
Canny
This multi-stage edge detector uses a filter based on the derivative of a Gaussian in order to compute the intensity of the gradients.
Note The settings for this filter include the option to select the low and high thresholds for hysteresis thresholding. Hysteresis thresholding on the gradient
magnitude determines which edge pixels are kept or removed from the output.
Close
This morphology filter smooths objects and fills-in small holes by performing dilation
followed by erosion using the same structuring element for both operations.
Dilate
This morphology filter enlarges the boundaries of regions of foreground pixels,
typically white pixels, using a structuring element.
DoG (Difference of Gaussian)
This edge detection filter first performs a Gaussian blur at a specified standard deviation (first sigma) and then another blur less than the first (second sigma). The final image is then calculated by replacing each pixel with the difference between the two blurred images and detecting where the values cross zero.
Erode
This morphology filter erodes away the boundaries of regions of foreground pixels, typically white pixels, using a structuring element.
Gaussian
This smoothing filter applies a convolution operation with a Gaussian filter kernel to smooth images.
Kuwahara
This smoothing filter provides non-linear smoothing for adaptive noise reduction.
Laplacian
This edge detection filter highlights the regions in which there is a rapid intensity change using a discrete convolution kernel that approximates the second derivatives of the image in the definition of the Laplacian.
Mean
This smoothing filter replaces each pixel with the mean value of its neighbors.
Median
This smoothing filter replaces each pixel with the median value of its neighbors, which can be highly effective on salt-and-pepper noise.
Non-local means
A 3D version of the non-local means filter, which smoothes images by taking a mean of all pixels weighted by how similar the pixels are to the target pixel.
Open
This morphology filter performs an erosion operation, followed by a dilation to smooth objects and remove isolated pixels.
Sobel
This edge detection filter named after Irwin Sobel creates an image which emphasizes edges and transitions.
Note The GPGPU version of the Sobel filter was updated to the 'classical' version of this filter.
Unsharp
This filter sharpens an image by subtracting a blurred version of itself from the original.
GPGPU Acceleration for Processing Images
The following items are available for executing operations on images within the GPGPU framework.
Available GPGPU operations for processing images
Process
Description
Surface determination
Accelerates surface determination for the generation of precise meshes (see Surface Determination Tool for additional information).
GPGPU Acceleration for Processing ROIs
The following items are available for executing operations on regions of interest within the GPGPU framework. In some cases, you may notice minor differences in the outputs of GPGPU versus CPU processing. This is due to the differences between the algorithms implemented.
Available GPGPU operations for regions of interest
Operation
Description
Ambient occlusion (AO) fields
Used for segmenting pores and cavities in 3D images (see Ambient Occlusion (AO) Fields for additional information about this algorithm).
3D thinning
This operation for skeletonization, which is a preliminary step for computing
graphs, is accelerated within the GPGPU framework.
Note Although the overall shapes of skeletons generated from GPU and CPU processing are usually identical to each other, the GPU-based result often contains fewer unnecessary branches.
Distance maps
Distance map computations, which are used in a number of transform processes, are accelerated within the GPGPU framework.
Ultimate erode
This operation automatically creates a seed multi-ROI that finds the centers of mass of the objects within a region of interest that would be separated by segmentation (see Creating Seeds with Ultimate Erodes).

documents.title: Installing Dragonfly
documents.text:
Installing Dragonfly
The following instructions provide information for installing Dragonfly 3D World. You should note that installation is a two-part process. The required distribution will be installed first and then Dragonfly 3D World. If you are a Python user, the private installation of the distribution should not disrupt your regular use of Python.
You should review the recommendations in the topic System Recommendations to make sure that your system can handle the large datasets, intensive computations, and high memory throughput demanded by Dragonfly 3D World.
Installing Dragonfly on Windows
Refer to the following instructions for information about installing Dragonfly 3D World on Windows systems.
How to Install Dragonfly on Windows
Log onto the client computer with administrator privileges, recommended.
Double-click the Dragonfly installer you downloaded. For example, InstallDragonfly3DWorld_2063.exe.
Note If the User Account Control dialog appears, you will need to enter an admin username and password to allow the program to make changes to your computer.
The Dragonfly 3D World Setup Wizard appears.
Click Next in the Dragonfly Setup Wizard to begin the update.
The License Agreement screen appears.
Review the license agreement and then click I Agree if you accept the terms.
Note You cannot install the program without first accepting the license agreement.
The Choose Components screen appears.
Select the optional components you want to install — a program group and/or a desktop shortcut.
Click Next to continue.
The Install Dragonfly screen appears.
Select the required option for creating shortcuts — All users or Current user only.
Click Next to continue.
The Choose Install Location screen appears.
.
By default, the program will be installed in C:\Program Files\Dragonfly\.
To install the program in a different folder, click the Browse button and then select another folder in the Browse For Folder dialog.
Click Install to start the installation.
Wait for the first part of the process — extraction and installation of the Python distribution — to be completed.
Wait for the second part of the process — installation of Dragonfly 3D World — to be completed.
Note One of the last steps of the installation process, which is identified as 'Adjusting write permissions…', can be lengthy on some systems. This is normal and you must be patient.
Click Next when installation of Dragonfly 3D World is complete.
Do the following, as required.
Check Show Release Notes, optional. If checked, the release notes for the installed version will appear in Adobe Acrobat Reader.
Click Finish to complete the setup of Dragonfly.
The Welcome to Dragonfly web page appears. And if selected, the release notes for the installed version will appear.

documents.title: NVIDIA Settings for 3D Rendering Performance
documents.text:
NVIDIA Settings for 3D Rendering Performance
To achieve optimal 3D rendering performance in Dragonfly when using an NVIDIA graphic adapter — either a GTX, RTX or Quadro — a number of program-specific 3D settings are highly recommended. The primary advantages include enhanced 3D rendering speed, optimal GPU utilization, high-performance for texture filtering, and other benefits.
These settings, which let you optimize GPU performance for Dragonfly’s specific demands without affecting global system settings, are applied automatically when you install Dragonfly 3D World.
You can review the program-specific settings for Dragonfly 3D World on the Program Settings tab in the NVIDIA Control Panel, as shown below.
Manage 3D Settings
How to Review the 3D Settings for Dragonfly 3D World
Open the NVIDIA Control Panel.
Go to 3D Settings > Manage 3D Settings in the NVIDIA Control Panel.
Click the Program Settings tab.
Choose Dragonfly 3D World (dragonfly.exe) in the 'Select a program to customize' drop-down menu, as shown below.
Note Information about the 3D settings is available on NVIDIA’s Manage 3D Settings reference web page (www.nvidia.com/content/Control-Panel-Help/vLatest/en-us/mergedProjects/nv3d/ Manage_3D_Settings_(reference).htm).
The program-specific settings for Dragonfly 3D World are configured as shown below. Program-specific settings are indicated in bold text.

documents.title: Optimizing Performance
documents.text:
Optimizing Performance
A number of settings are recommended to help optimize the performance of Dragonfly 3D World. These are summarized below.
You can also review the recommendations in the topic System Recommendations to make sure that your system can handle the large datasets, intensive computations, and high memory throughput demanded by Dragonfly 3D World.
NVIDIA settings for 3D rendering performance… Provides a list of critical settings that achieve optimal 3D rendering performance in Dragonfly when using an NVIDIA graphic adapter — either a GTX, RTX or Quadro (see NVIDIA Settings for 3D Rendering Performance).
Graphic settings for high performance… Lists the custom graphics settings available in Windows that can improve application performance (see Custom Graphics Settings for High Performance).
Power plan for high performance… Provides instructions for selecting a power plan that favors high performance, helps eliminate power-saving bottlenecks and ensures that the CPU and GPU operate at their maximum potential (see Setting a Custom Power Plan for High Performance).

documents.title: Reporting Issues
documents.text:
Reporting Issues
Dragonfly includes an integrated reporting module that lets you report issues directly to the Support Team. For example, when an unknown error occurs or if an unexpected result is generated.
Choose Help > Report an Issue on the menu bar to open the Report an Issue dialog, shown below.
Report an Issue dialog
Try to include as much information as possible to help the Support Team to understand why the issue occurred. You can enter details about the issue, such as how to reproduce the problem, send the log and installation logs, as well as upload a file, such as a screen capture, video, or text document, that further describes your issue.
Sending Reports to Support Team
Dragonfly includes an integrated reporting module that lets you report any issue that results in a crash. Whenever you choose to send a crash report, try to include as much information as possible to help the support team to understand why the issue occurred. You can enter details about the issue, such as how to reproduce the problem, in the Send Report to Support Team dialog. Whenever you choose to send a crash report, try to include as much information as possible to help the support team to understand why the issue occurred. You can enter details about the issue, such as how to reproduce the problem, in the Send Report to Support Team dialog.

documents.title: Requesting Non-Commercial (FreeD) Licenses
documents.text:
Requesting Non-Commercial (FreeD) Licenses
To use Dragonfly for non-commercial purposes after your trial version has expired, you will need to request and then activate a non-commercial license. Non-commercial 'FreeD' licenses are granted free-of-charge to qualified researchers, academics, students, and non-commercial developers for non-profit research, academic, or development purposes. Non-commercial licenses are valid for a one-year period and can be renewed annually at no charge. Details are available on the FreeD License web page).
Choose Help > Request Non-Commercial License on the menu bar to open the Dragonfly User Survey webpage, shown below. You will need to enter your credentials and complete the survey to request a non-commercial license. You should note that license keys will be sent to the submitted email.
Dragonfly User Survey webpage
Make sure you have a photo of the ID issued by your institute or research facility before you begin. Acceptable file formats are JPEG, PNG, and BMP.
How to Request a Non-Commercial License
Do one of the following:
Choose Help > Request Non-Commercial License on the menu bar.
Click Request Non-Commercial License in the License Expired message box.
This message box will appear onscreen if your Dragonfly license has already expired and the application is locked.
The Dragonfly User Survey webpage appears.
Click the Information and Terms of Service link to review the non-commercial licensing program requirements, recommended.
Enter your credentials, attach a photo of the ID issued by your institution or organization, and then complete the survey.
Submit your request.
Our team will review the information provided in the submitted survey. If approved, your requested license key will be sent to the submitted email. You will then need to activate your new license (see Activating Dragonfly).

documents.title: Requesting Support
documents.text:
Requesting Support
If you are a currently covered by a valid maintenance and support plan, you can contact our Support Team directly through the Dragonfly interface to request support. You can also create a support ticket in the Dragonfly Helpdesk (helpdesk.theobjects.com/support/home). A maintenance and support plan is the best way to ensure you have access to technical support resources when it matters most.
Before contacting us, please check if your request has already been answered either in the Dragonfly Helpdesk (helpdesk.theobjects.com/support/home), Dragonfly Social (see Connecting to Dragonfly Social), or in this Help system.
How to Request Support
Choose Help > Request Support on the menu bar.
Enter your name, email, and your request in the appropriate fields.
Upload a file or files, such as a screen capture, video, or text document, that further describes your inquiry, optional.
Click the Submit button to send your request.

documents.title: Setting a Custom Power Plan for High Performance
documents.text:
Setting a Custom Power Plan for High Performance
Setting 'High performance' as the custom power plan for Dragonfly helps eliminate power-saving bottlenecks, which helps ensure that the CPU and GPU operate at maximum potential rather than ramping down during minor lulls in workloads. This setting helps resolve, or prevent, performance issues like lags and micro-stutters, as well as reduce overall rendering times.
The 'High performance' setting, circled below, is available in the Control Panel, as shown below.
Power Options
How to Change the Power Plan
Go to Control Panel > System and Security.
Click Power Options, as shown below.
The Power Options settings appear.
Select the High performance setting, as shown below.
Do the following if the High performance setting is not available:
Click Change plan settings on the Power Options screen.
Click Change advanced power settings on the Edit Plan Settings screen, as shown below.
The Power Options dialog appears.
Choose High performance in the drop-down menu, as shown below, and then apply and save the change.
You will then be able to pick 'High performance' as the preferred plan on the Power Options screen.

documents.title: System Recommendations
documents.text:
System Recommendations
Running Dragonfly 3D World often requires more than just a standard computer setup — it calls for a carefully balanced system designed to handle large datasets, intensive computations, and high memory throughput. Choosing the right configuration can significantly improve performance, responsiveness, as well as overall workflow efficiency.
In this topic, key recommendations for building or selecting a computer system capable of meeting these challenges are outlined, focusing on critical components such as the graphic processing unit (GPU), memory capacity, CPU performance, memory capacity, and storage speed.
You can also find additional information about the System Requirements for Dragonfly 3D World on our website (dragonfly.comet.tech/en/support-and-training/system-requirements).
GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)
You should select a GPU from the most recent generation available (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 50-series). Although higher VRAM can be beneficial, it is not always necessary to choose the highest-capacity model if budget constraints are a concern. Prioritizing newer architectures is generally more advantageous.
Consumer-grade GPUs (gaming-oriented models) are significantly more cost-effective than workstation-class GPUs and typically provide more than sufficient performance for most users.
RAM (Memory)
You should opt for high-speed memory, preferably DDR5 with a minimum speed of approximately 4400 MT/s. The required capacity will depend on specific workflows. A good guideline is to provision RAM at roughly three times the size of your dataset.
For example, if a dataset consumes 10 GB of RAM when loaded into Dragonfly, a system with approximately 64 GB of RAM is recommended. It is important to consider the in-memory size reported by the software rather than the file size on disk, as storage formats may be compressed, whereas RAM usage reflects the full, uncompressed data footprint.
CPU (Processor)
Modern consumer CPUs from either Intel or AMD are suitable choices. Emphasis should be placed on higher clock speeds rather than a higher core count, as many operations in Dragonfly benefit more from strong single-core performance. While some tasks can utilize multiple cores, overall performance tends to scale better with faster individual cores.
Windows operating systems typically support up to 64 cores per application, whereas Linux does not impose this limitation.
Motherboard
The motherboard should be selected to fully support the capabilities of the GPU, RAM, and CPU. This includes compatibility with desired memory speeds, processor performance, and expansion requirements. Investing in high-performance components without ensuring motherboard compatibility can result in underutilized hardware and unnecessary expense.
Storage (Hard Drive)
High-speed NVMe solid-state drives are strongly recommended. Although they may be more expensive depending on capacity, they can significantly reduce data loading times and improve overall system responsiveness. Slow storage can become a major bottleneck, particularly when working with large datasets.

documents.title: Transferring Dragonfly Licenses
documents.text:
Transferring Dragonfly Licenses
This topic describes how you can move your Dragonfly licenses from one computer to another when both systems are connected to the internet. As described below, you must first deactivate the currently licensed version of Dragonfly before transferring your software licenses to a new computer and activating them again.
If you don't have access to your old computer anymore, contact the Support Team to deactivate the licenses for you (see Requesting Support). You may also need to contact the Support Team if you need to deactivate/activate Dragonfly on offline systems (see Activating Dragonfly Offline).
How to Transfer Dragonfly Licenses
Do the following to deactivate the licenses on the old computer:
Choose Help > Activate Product on the menu bar.
The Activate Product dialog appears.
Click the Deactivate button in the Activate Product dialog, as circled below.
Install Dragonfly on the new computer, if not already done (see Installing Dragonfly).
Transfer the license(s) to the new computer as follows:
Choose Help > Activate Product on the menu bar.
The Activate Product dialog appears.
Activate the licenses on the new computer (see Activating Dragonfly).
Important You must always deactivate your licenses first. If you did not deactivate your licenses before activating them on your new computer, the activation will fail and you will not be able to use Dragonfly.

documents.title: Updating Dragonfly
documents.text:
Updating Dragonfly
All Dragonfly customers receive notification of new software releases, which contain new features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and other important changes.
Commercial users must have a valid Maintenance and Support plan to be eligible for a new version. Non-commercial users must have a current non-commercial license.
How to Update Dragonfly
Log onto the client computer with administrator privileges, recommended.
Double-click the Dragonfly installer you downloaded. For example,
InstallDragonfly3DWorld_2081.exe.
Note If the User Account Control dialog appears, you may need to enter an admin username and password to allow the program to make changes to your computer.
The Dragonfly Setup Wizard appears.
Click Next to begin the update.
The License Agreement screen appears.
Review the license agreement, and, if you accept the terms, click I Agree to continue.
Note You cannot update the program without first accepting the license agreement.
The Install Dragonfly screen appears.
Do one of the following:
Select Overwrite existing installation if want to simply update the current version of Dragonfly.
Select Overwrite another existing installation if you have multiple instances of Dragonfly and you want to overwrite one of those versions. You can enter the path to the installation folder of the version you want to overwrite or you can click Browse and then choose the folder in the Browse For Folder dialog.
Click Update to continue.
Wait for the update to be completed and the Installation Complete screen to appear.
Review the installation summary, recommended, and then click Next on the Installation Complete screen.
The Completing Dragonfly Setup screen appears.
Do the following, as required.
Check Show Release Notes, optional. If checked, the release notes for the installed version will appear in Adobe Acrobat Reader.
Click Finish to complete the setup of your new version of Dragonfly.

documents.title: Additive Noise Filter
documents.text:
Additive Noise Filter
The Additive Noise filter lets you artificially add noise to an image. Deliberately corrupting an image with noise can let you test the resistance of an image processing operator to noise and assess the performance of various noise reduction filters and denoising models.
The result of adding noise to a grayscale image is show below on an intensity profile.
Intensity profile
The following options are available for the Additive noise filter in the Image Processing panel.
Options for additive noise
Distribution… Lets you choose a distribution for the added noise — Uniform absolute, Uniform relative, and Gaussian.
Range… Lets you choose the range of data within which noise will be added. For example, at a range of 100 with a Uniform relative distribution, noise will be added within ±50 of the original data.

documents.title: Applying Saved Operations
documents.text:
Applying Saved Operations
To help accelerate repetitive post-processing tasks, you can import a saved image filtering workflow and then apply that operation directly to selected image data. This option is available in the Image Processing panel, which is available on the Main tab of the left sidebar and is shown below.
Image Processing panel
How to Apply a Saved Operation
Select the required image data in the Dataset drop-down menu.
Do one of the following, as required:
Select the required operation in the Recent Ops drop-down menu.
Click the Refresh button to update the list of saved image processing operations.
Check the Create new dataset option if you want to create a new dataset as a result of the applied operation.
If not selected, the original input image data will be modified.
Click the Apply button to process the selected image data.
If required, you can click the Advanced button to open the Image Processing window (see Image Filtering Window).

documents.title: Arithmetic Operations
documents.text:
Arithmetic Operations
Simple arithmetic operations, which can be applied as a preliminary step in complex image processing sequences and also as operators in their own right, are applied in a pixel-by-pixel fashion. This means that the value of a pixel in the output image depends only on the values of the corresponding pixels in the input image or images. For example, the result of an addition is that each pixel value in the output dataset is the sum of the values of the corresponding pixel from each of the input images. A main advantage of arithmetic operators is that these processes are very simple and usually quite fast.
The Arithmetic filter allows you to select a number of inputs and then write an expression to produce an output. For example, addition can be used to add components from one image into another image, subtraction can be used for change detection, and multiplication can be used to increase the average gray level of an image by multiplying it with a constant. The convention for identifying each input within an expression is simply "A" for the first dataset, "B" for the second dataset, "C" for the third, and so on. For example, to get the sum of the first dataset and the second dataset, the expression would be "A+B". More complex expressions can also be written, such as "D*[(A+B)+(2*A-1.8*B)]/C.
You can also include NumPy functionalities in an expression. For example, in the expression "np.sin(A)+np.cos(B)", "np.sin" and "np.cos" refer to the "sine" and "cosine" functions of NumPy. NumPy is the fundamental package for scientific computing in Python. At the core of the NumPy package, is the ndarray (N-dimensional array) object, which has a fixed size at creation. NumPy arrays facilitate advanced mathematical and other types of operations on large numbers of data. Typically, such operations are executed more efficiently and with less code than is possible using Python’s built-in sequences.
Unless you choose to work with the Advanced Options, all inputs in arithmetic operations must have the same characteristics — size, location, spacing, orientation and data type— to be used in the same workflow. See Working with the Advanced Options for more information about multi-scale image processing.
To avoid any wrapping of pixel values and for best precision, all calculations for arithmetic operations are done in float. You should note that if you set an output as another data type when working with the Advanced options, all calculations will still be done in float. However, in such cases, the output data values will be rounded and may be clipped.
References
[1] https://www.numpy.org/
[2] https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/

documents.title: Contrast Adjustment Filters
documents.text:
Contrast Adjustment Filters
These filters, which include CLAHE, Histogram Equalization, Local Histogram Equalization, Normalization, and Slope Map, can be used to adjust the contrast in images by remapping the gray scale or by recalculating the range of values in an image.
Contrast adjustment filters and settings
What it does
Settings
CLAHE
Adaptive histogram equalization (AHE) is a computer image processing technique used to improve contrast in images. It differs from ordinary histogram equalization in the respect that the adaptive method computes several histograms, each corresponding to a distinct section of the image, and uses them to redistribute the lightness values of the image. It is therefore suitable for improving the local contrast and enhancing the definitions of edges in each region of an image. However, AHE has a tendency to overamplify noise in relatively homogeneous regions of an image.
This variant of adaptive histogram equalization called CLAHE (contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization) prevents this by limiting the amplification. In the case of CLAH, the contrast limiting procedure is applied for each neighborhood from which a transformation function is derived.
Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptive_histogram_equalization
Clip
Nb tiles
Bins
Histogram Equalization
Histogram equalization is a contrast enhancement technique in which the gray scale is remapped so that the output image uses the entire range available and there are approximately the same number of pixels of each gray value in the output image. The equalized image has a roughly linear cumulative distribution function.
You should note that the effectiveness of using the same number of pixels for each gray value must be judged empirically. You should also note that this operation can cause large homogeneous regions to be remapped into more gray levels. This may or may not help in image interpretation.
While histogram equalization has the advantage that it requires no parameters, it sometimes yields unnatural looking images. An alternative method is local histogram equalization.
Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histogram_equalization
-
Local Histogram Equalization
Enhances images with low contrast by spreading out the most frequent intensity values in an image. While equalized images have a roughly linear cumulative distribution function for each pixel neighborhood, the local version of histogram equalization emphasizes local gray level variations.
Reference: https://scikit-image.org/docs/dev/auto_examples/color_exposure/plot_local_equalize.html?highlight=local%20histogram%20equalization
Kernel size
Normalization
Normalization is a process that recalculates the range of pixel values in an image so that it is equal to the maximum range for the data type. For example, 0 to 255 for 8-bit images, 0 to 65535 for 16-bit images, and 0 to 1.0 for float images. This contrast stretch is similar to the Auto Contrast option in Adobe Photoshop and is often referred to as dynamic range expansion. For example, if the intensity range of the image is 50 to 180 and the desired range is 0 to 255 the process entails subtracting 50 from each of pixel intensity, making the range 0 to 130. Then each pixel intensity is multiplied by 255/130, making the range 0 to 255.
The purpose of dynamic range expansion is usually to bring the image, or other type of signal, into a range that is more familiar or normal, hence the term normalization. Often, the motivation is to achieve consistency in dynamic range for a set of data.
-
Slope Map
Relies on the blurring effects of a Gaussian filter to quantify underlying local trends characterizing image intensity and balance contrast. This filter can remove vignetting artifacts quite effectively.
It is also equivalent to a local histogram equalization without priors if a global histogram equalization is applied to the slope map afterwards. It typically works well on mammogram and X-ray images.

documents.title: Edge Detection Filters
documents.text:
Edge Detection Filters
The edge detection filters available in Dragonfly can be used to emphasize the edges and transitions in an image. Edges are usually one of the most important features in a structure, and can often be used for measurements after appropriate edge detection has been applied.
Edge detection filter comparison
Original image
Difference of Gaussian (DoG)
Laplacian
Sobel
Edge detection filters and settings
What it does
Settings
Canny
The Canny filter is a multi-stage edge detector. It uses a filter based on the derivative of a Gaussian in order to compute the intensity of the gradients. The Gaussian reduces the effect of noise present in the image. Then, potential edges are thinned down to 1-pixel curves by removing non-maximum pixels of the gradient magnitude. Finally, edge pixels are kept or removed using hysteresis thresholding on the gradient magnitude.
References
[1] https://scikit-image.org/docs/dev/auto_examples/edges/plot_canny.html?highlight=canny
[2] Canny, J., A Computational Approach To Edge Detection, IEEE Trans. Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 8:679-714, 1986
Sigma
DoG (Difference of Gaussian)
Performs a Gaussian blur on an image at a specified standard deviation (first sigma). The resulting image is a blurred version of the source image. The module then performs another blur that blurs the image less than previously (second sigma). The final image is then calculated by replacing each pixel with the difference between the two blurred images and detecting when the values cross zero. The resulting zero crossings will be focused at edges or areas of pixels that have some variation in their surrounding neighborhood.
First sigma
Second sigma
Normalized
Laplacian
The Laplacian filter highlights the regions in which there is a rapid intensity change using a discrete convolution kernel that approximates the second derivatives of the image in the definition of the Laplacian. The Laplacian enhancement operation generates sharp peaks at the edges, and any brightness slope, regardless of whether it is positive or negative, is accentuated.
References
[1] https://www.tutorialspoint.com/dip/Laplacian_Operator.htm
-
Prewitt
Finds the horizontal and/or vertical edges of an image using the Prewitt transform.
References
[1] https://scikit-image.org/docs/dev/api/skimage.filters.html?highlight=prewitt#skimage.filters.prewitt_h
[2] https://scikit-image.org/docs/dev/api/skimage.filters.html?highlight=prewitt#skimage.filters.prewitt_v
Direction
Scharr
Finds the horizontal and/or vertical edges of an image using the Scharr transform.
References
[1] https://scikit-image.org/docs/dev/api/skimage.filters.html?highlight=prewitt#skimage.filters.scharr_h
[2] https://scikit-image.org/docs/dev/api/skimage.filters.html?highlight=prewitt#skimage.filters.scharr_v
[3] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobel_operator#Alternative_operators
Direction
Sobel
The Sobel filter, which is named after Irwin Sobel, creates an image which emphasizes edges and transitions. It is a discrete differentiation operator that computes an approximation of the gradient of the image intensity function. At each point in the image, the result of the Sobel operator is either the corresponding gradient vector or the norm of this vector. The Sobel operator is based on convolving the image with a small, separable, and integer valued filter in the horizontal and vertical directions. Although these convolutions can be very useful for edge enhancement of images captured in microscopes, the gradient approximation that it produces is often relatively crude, in particular for high frequency variations in the image.
Derivative filters provide a quantitative measurement for the rate of change in pixel brightness information present in an image. When a derivative filter is applied, the resulting data concerning brightness fluctuation rates can be used to enhance contrast, detect edges and boundaries, and to measure feature orientation. One of the most important derivative filters is the Sobel filter, which is based on a convolution operation that can produce a derivative in any of eight directions.
References
[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobel_operator
Apply Gaussian Before Sobel

An important issue that arises within the convolution process centers on the fact that the convolution kernel will extend beyond the borders of the image when it is applied to border pixels. A common approach to dealing with border effects is to pad the original image with extra rows and columns based on the filter size. The technique used in Dragonfly to remedy border effects is to reflect the image at the borders. For example, column[-1] = column [1], column [-2] = column [2], and so on. For more information, go to https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/rbf/HIPR2/convolve.htm and https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/rbf/HIPR2/kernel.htm.
How to Create a Custom Convolution Filter
Choose Tools > Image Processing Toolbox on the menu bar.
Choose Convolution as the operation.
Select a kernel shape and size in the Options box.
Enter the required matrix values.
Select or de-select the Normalize option, as required.
Preview the filtering effect of the customized kernel, recommended (see Previewing Operations).
If required, you can modify the matrix values or choose another shape.
Save the operation, recommended (see Saving and Loading Image Filtering Operations).

documents.title: Angular Count
documents.text:
Angular Count
Number of circularly symmetric neighbor set points (quantization of the angular space).

documents.title: Compensation
documents.text:
Compensation
Available for the Local Entropy Minimization, Polynomial Third Degree, and Radial Basis Function filters, this parameter controls contrast after fitting for shading correction.
Effects of compensation for shading operations
Divide… The effect of selecting this parameter for shading operations is that contrast will be retained, particularly for like materials, after the shading operation is completed.
Subtract… In general, local contrast may be lost when this parameter is selected for shading operations.

documents.title: Gradient Magnitude Threshold (K)
documents.text:
Gradient Magnitude Threshold (K)
The gradient magnitude threshold, K, controls the rate of the diffusion and serves as a soft threshold between the image gradients that are attributed to noise and those attributed to edges.

documents.path: Image Filtering/Filter Settings/Kernel Shape and Size.htm
documents.title: Kernel Shape and Size
documents.text:
Kernel Shape and Size
Convolution filters are based around a kernel, which represents the shape and size of the neighborhood that will be sampled when calculating the pixel values to be modified. Convolution filters, as the name implies, perform a convolution of the filter coefficients with the input data. The basic idea is that a window of some finite size and shape — the kernel — is scanned across the image. The output pixel value is the weighted sum of the input pixels within the window where the weights are the values of the filter assigned to every pixel of the window itself. The window with its weights is called the convolution kernel (go to https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/rbf/HIPR2/convolve.htm for more information).
Various standard kernels are provided for convolution-based image filters and the size and the form of the kernel determine the characteristics of the operation. A simple 5 x 5 structuring element and the shapes available for 2D interpretation are shown below.
Simple structuring elements
You should note that the size of the neighborhood controls the amount of filtering. A larger neighborhood, corresponding to a larger convolution mask, will result in a greater degree of filtering. You should also note that as a trade-off for greater amounts of smoothing, for example, larger neighborhoods may also result in a loss of image detail.
An important issue that arises within the convolution process centers on the fact that the convolution kernel will extend beyond the borders of the image when it is applied to border pixels. A common approach to dealing with border effects is to pad the original image with extra rows and columns based on the filter size. The technique used in Dragonfly to remedy border effects is to reflect the image at the borders. For example, column[-1] = column [1], column [-2] = column [2], and so on.

documents.path: Image Filtering/Filter Settings/Maximum Width in Pixels.htm
documents.title: Maximum Width in Pixels
documents.text:
Maximum Width in Pixels
Maximum width of the rings to be filtered in pixels.

documents.title: Method of Thresholding
documents.text:
Method of Thresholding
The method used to determine the adaptive threshold for the local neighborhood in weighted mean image. Methods include Gaussian, mean, and median. By default the 'Gaussian' method is used.

documents.title: Method
documents.text:
Method
Lets you choose a method to determine the pattern:
default… Original local binary pattern which is grayscale invariant but not rotation invariant.
ror… Extension of default pattern which is grayscale invariant and rotation invariant.
uniform… Uniform pattern which is grayscale invariant and rotation invariant and offers finer quantization of the angular space.
var… Variance of local image texture (related to contrast) which is rotation invariant but not grayscale invariant.

documents.path: Image Filtering/Filter Settings/Minimum Angle in Degrees.htm
documents.title: Minimum Angle in Degrees
documents.text:
Minimum Angle in Degrees
Features larger than twice this angle (degrees) will be considered a ring artifact. Must be less than 180 degrees.

documents.title: Mode
documents.text:
Mode
The mode — Soft or Hard — determines the type of thresholding to be applied on the input data.

documents.path: Image Filtering/Filter Settings/Node Count and Iteration Count.htm
documents.title: Node Count and Iteration Count
documents.text:
Node Count and Iteration Count
This parameter determines how many nodes will be scanned across the image to determine the best fit and how many times the nodes will be scanned.
Node count… Determines how many nodes will be scanned across the image. For example, if a Node count of 5 is selected, then 25 nodes will scanned across the image (5 in the X axis and 5 in the Y axis). In general, the Node count should be selected according to the particle size in your sample. In general, if your dataset contains large particles, you should select a limited number of nodes. If your dataset contains small particles, you can select a greater number of nodes.
Iteration count… This parameter determines the number of iterations that will be performed. The larger the number of iterations, the more precise shading correction will be. However, you must also consider the time required to complete each iteration.

documents.title: Noise
documents.text:
Noise
Available for the Mean Shift filter, this parameter allows you to limit intensity variations when computing the spatial center.

documents.title: Offset
documents.text:
Offset
Constant subtracted from weighted mean of neighborhood to calculate the local threshold value. You should note that the default offset is 0.

documents.title: Radius and Amount
documents.text:
Radius and Amount
The first step in the unsharp filtering process is to produce a blurred image with a Gaussian low-pass filter. Increasing the size of the Gaussian filter by its radius usually causes the Unsharp filter to produce a sharper image. You should note that the radius should fit inside the selected kernel.
Amount is simply how strong you want the sharpening to be. A low setting means that sharpening will be subtle, while higher settings will increase sharpening.

documents.title: Radius
documents.text:
Radius
Radius of the circle (spatial resolution of the operator).

documents.title: Rician Noise
documents.text:
Rician Noise
If selected for the Non-Local Means filter, shading correction will consider that Rician noise is present in the data.

documents.title: Sigma
documents.text:
Sigma
Standard deviation of the Gaussian filter used to smooth the image.

documents.title: Standard Deviation
documents.text:
Standard Deviation
Available for the Gaussian filter, this parameter determines the standard deviation of the Gaussian used for smoothing differences in intensities. The greater the value, the stronger the blur will be.

documents.title: Theta
documents.text:
Theta
Perhaps one of the most important parameters of the Gabor filter, this parameter decides what kind of features the filter responds to. For example, giving Theta a value of zero means that the filter is responsive only to horizontal features only.

documents.title: Unsharp Factor
documents.text:
Unsharp Factor
Controls the weight given to the edges.

documents.title: Wavelength
documents.text:
Wavelength
Is the wavelength of the sinusoidal factor used to compute the filter.

documents.title: Wavelets
documents.text:
Wavelets
The wavelets that you can select for the artifact removal filters and the wavelet smoothing filter are grouped by family. The properties of each family are listed in the table below.
Wavelet families and properties
Family
(Abbr.)
Properties
Biorthogonal
(bior)
Symmetric, not orthogonal, biorthogonal (see https://wavelets.pybytes.com/family/bior/).
Coiflets
(coif)
Near symmetric, orthogonal, biorthogonal (see https://wavelets.pybytes.com/family/coif/).
Daubechies
(db)
Asymmetric, orthogonal, biorthogonal (see https://wavelets.pybytes.com/family/db/).
Discrete Meyer (FIR Approximation)
(dmey)
Symmetric, orthogonal, biorthogonal (see https://wavelets.pybytes.com/family/dmey/).

Asymmetric, orthogonal, biorthogonal (see https://wavelets.pybytes.com/family/haar/).
Reverse Biorthogonal

For more information about Py Wavelets, refer to https://media.readthedocs.org/pdf/pywavelets/stable/pywavelets.pdf.

documents.title: Filter Types
documents.text:
Filter Types
Image filtering is one of the most fundamental operations of image processing and can greatly improve image quality and yield information that otherwise would have been missed. You should note that some filters are known for detecting or preserving edges, while others are typically used for smoothing or denoising. You should also note that filter performance is dependent both on the input image and on the parameters selected for filtering, such as kernel shape and size, iterations, and so on.
Sometimes the best results may be obtained by applying two or more filters sequentially. For example, you may need to preserve edges while smoothing uniform yet noisy areas. In the Image Processing panel, you can simply add sequential filtering operations to create a composite filter. However, you should be careful to note your order of operations as some filters may be contradictory and may not always be simply applied sequentially.
You can also easily create your own specialized filters with the Simple Dataset Filter Generator.
The table below provides a brief description of each type of image filter available in Dragonfly.
Image filter types
What they do
Arithmetic
Lets select a number of inputs and then write an expression to produce an output (see Arithmetic Operations).
Two filters — Gradient and Divergence — are also available in the Arithmetic category to extract information from images. The Gradient filter lets you compute the gradient along a selected axis, while the Divergence filter, which is the inverse of the Gradient filter, indicates minor grayscale variations.
Artifact Removal
These filters can be used to remove stripes and ring artifacts from image data (see Artifact Removal Filters).
Contrast
These filters can be used to adjust the contrast in images by remapping the grayscale or by recalculating the range of values in an image (see Contrast Adjustment Filters).
Detector
These filters emphasize the edges and transitions in an image (see Detector Filters).
Edge Detection
These filters emphasize the edges and transitions in an image (see Edge Detection Filters).
Editable
Lets you create your own filter effects — smoothing, sharpening, intensifying, enhancing — with a customized kernel for convolution (see Editable Filter).
Frequency Domain
Two filters — Discrete Fourier Transform and Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform — are available for transforming time domain signals to the frequency domain and for inverting transformed signals (see Frequency Domain Filters).
Information
The Entropy filter can be used to detect subtle variations in the local grayscale distribution.
Morphology
Morphological operators — dilate, erode, open, and close — can be applied through image filtering to grow or shrink image regions, as well as to remove or fill-in image region boundary pixels (see Morphology Filters).
Additive Noise
Lets you artificially add noise to an image (see Additive Noise Filter).
Segmentation
These filters — K-Means and Mini-Batch K-Means — can be used to partition an image into a specific number of meaningful regions (see Segmentation Filters).
Shading Compensation
These filters can be used to correct undesirable shading across the field-of-view, which can be a prominent phenomenon in microscopy and may occur due to non-uniform illumination, inhomogeneous detector sensitivity, or non-specific sample staining (see Shading Compensation Filters).
Sharpening
These filters can be used to emphasize the details in an image and enhance the edges of objects (see Sharpening Filters).
Smoothing
These filters can be applied to reduce the amount of noise in an image (see Smoothing Filters).
Texture Analysis
Texture analysis characterizes the texture of a region by quantifying spatial variation in pixel intensities (see Texture Analysis Filters).
Thresholding
Thresholding filters output an image composed of two basic classes — foreground and background. These images can be used as masks for segmentation purposes or for other image processing tasks (see Thresholding Filters).

documents.title: Filtering Images
documents.text:
Filtering Images
You can filter images by applying standard image filters, comprehensive filters, and arithmetic operations. You should note that some filters are known for detecting or preserving edges, while others are typically used for smoothing or denoising (see Filter Types). If required, you can work in Advanced Mode, which lets you specify an output data type as well as work with multi-scale images (see Working with the Advanced Options).
Sometimes the best results may be obtained by applying two or more filters sequentially. For example, you may need to preserve edges while smoothing uniform yet noisy areas. In the Image Processing panel, you can simply add sequential filtering operations to create a composite filter. However, you should be careful to note your order of operations as some filters may be contradictory and may not always be simply applied sequentially.
How to Filter Images
Choose Workflows > Image Filtering on the menu bar.
The Image Filtering panel appears in a contextual window that includes a preview window and the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Image Filtering Window).
If required, you can import image data by clicking the Import Image Files button.
See Importing Image Files for information about importing image data.
Do the following, as required:
Add a standard image filter or multiple filters as the operation (see Adding Standard Image Filters).
Add an arithmetic operation (see Adding Arithmetic Operations).
Preview the effect of the selected operation(s), recommended (see Previewing Operations).
Apply the selected operations to modify the selected dataset or to create a new dataset (see Applying Operations).
Adding Standard Image Filters
You can add standard image filters to your filtering operation to detect edges, smooth or denoise images, or apply a threshold (see Filter Types). You should note that filter performance is dependent both on the input image and on the parameters selected for filtering, such as kernel shape and size, iterations, and interpretation.
How to Add a Standard Image Filter
Choose the required filter in the Operation drop-down list.
If an operations box is not available, click the Add Operation button.
Select an input in the Inputs drop-down list.
An output name, based on the input dataset and selected operation, appears automatically in the Outputs box.
Note You can rename the output, if required. Simply click inside the Outputs box and then enter the required name.
Do the following if you need to work in Advanced mode:
Check Advanced options in the Operations box, as shown below.
Additional output options appear in the Outputs box, circled below.
Select an output data type — Default, uint8 (unsigned 8 bits), uint16 ( unsigned short 16 bits), uint32 (unsigned integer 32 bits), or float32 (float 32 bits) — in the Data type drop-down menu, if required.
Note Changing the output data type to float may be required to prevent unwanted loss of precision or clipping. For example, the Laplacian filter normally produces negative values. If an unsigned data type is used as the output, the negative values will be lost. This could produce an incomprehensible result. Note that 'Default' is the data type of the first input.
Select an output geometry in the Geometry drop-down menu. You can choose the geometry of any object based on a structured grid — image data, region of interest, or multi-ROI — that is available in the Data Properties and Settings panel. You can also choose to keep the default shape, which is defined by the first input of your image processing workflow.
Choose the settings for the selected filter in the Options box.
Add additional operations to your processing workflow, if required.
Click the Add Operation button to add an operation. You can use the output of an operation as the input to another operation.
Preview the effect of the selected operation(s), recommended (see Previewing Operations).
Apply the selected operations to modify the selected dataset or to create a new dataset (see Applying Operations).
Save your image filtering workflow, optional (see Saving and Loading Image Filtering Operations).
Adding Arithmetic Operations
The Arithmetic filter allows you to select a number of inputs and then write an expression to produce an output (see Arithmetic Operations for additional information about arithmetic operations).
How to Add an Arithmetic Operation
Choose Arithmetic in the Operation drop-down list.
If an operations box is not available, click the Add Operation button.
Choose the number of inputs required for the arithmetic expression in the Inputs drop-down list.
Select the required input(s) in the Inputs drop-down lists. Inputs can be imported image data, as well as the outputs from other current image processing operations. Unless you are working with the Advanced Options, all inputs must have the same characteristics — size, location, spacing, orientation and data type — to be used simultaneously in an image processing workflow.
An output name, based on the input dataset and operation, appears automatically in the Outputs box.
Note You can rename the output, if required, Simply click inside the output box and then enter the required name.
Do the following if you need to work in Advanced mode:
Check Advanced options in the Operations box, as shown below.
Additional output options appear in the Outputs box.
Select an output data type — Default, uint8 (unsigned 8 bits), uint16 ( unsigned short 16 bits), uint32 (unsigned integer 32 bits), or float32 (float 32 bits) — in the Data type drop-down menu, if required.
Note Changing the output data type to float may be required to prevent unwanted loss of precision or clipping.
Select an output geometry in the Geometry drop-down menu. You can choose the geometry of any object based on a structured grid — image data, region of interest, or multi-ROI — that is available in the Data Properties and Settings panel. You can also choose to keep the default shape, which is defined by the first input of your image processing workflow.
Enter a valid arithmetic expression for the required operation (see Arithmetic Operations).
The convention for identifying each input within an expression is simply "A" for the first dataset, "B" for the second dataset, "C" for the third, and so on.
Preview the effect of the selected operation(s), recommended (see Previewing Operations).
Apply the selected operations to modify the selected dataset or to create a new dataset (see Applying Operations).
Save your image processing workflow, optional (see Saving and Loading Image Filtering Operations).
Previewing Operations
You can create previews in the Image Filtering contextual window to evaluate the effects of applying selected operations at their current settings. This arrangement allows you to decide whether to proceed with the current filter or filter combination and their settings, or to adjust the selected filter or filter combination. Note that previews are limited to the currently displayed slice and the visible part of the image. To facilitate reviews, you can synchronize zoom, position, and window leveling between the original dataset and filtering previews.
If you need to evaluate filtering at different steps in a series of operations, you can fuse multiple previews in the Preview window. Toggling visibility or changing opacity will allow you view the different previews.
How to Preview Operations
Select the required synchronize options for the original view — Zoom, Position, and Window Level — in the Scenes Views Synchronizer panel, recommended.
When synchronized, the preview window will be synchronized with the view of the original image.
In the scene containing the original dataset, adjust the zoom factor and position, if required. Note that previews are applied to the visible portion of an image only.
You can use your mouse or the tools on the Manipulate and Window Leveling panels to make your adjustments (Using the Manipulate Tools, and Window Leveling).
Select the operation that you want to preview, if required.
Note The selected operation is highlighted in the Image Filtering panel.
Do one of the following:
Click the Compute Selected Preview button to view the effect of the selected operation on the visible portion of the input image data.
Click the Compute All Previews to compute and view the effect of all operations on the visible portion of the input image data.
The computed preview appears in the Preview window.
Evaluate the effect of the applied operation.
You can apply a 2D LUT to help visualize filtering effects (see 2D Settings). You can also add annotations, such as rulers and regions, to quantitatively evaluate filtering effects. For example, you can evaluate shading correction by comparing the intensity profiles of the original dataset with the filtered image (see Profiling Intensity).
Applying Operations
Processing operations can be applied by one of two mechanisms — either at the input so that the original image data is modifier, or at the output, so that a new dataset is created.
How to Apply an Operation
Review the outputs that are available in the Output box. By default, each operation within an image processing workflow is added as an output and is set to create a new dataset.
Remove any outputs that are not needed.
To remove an output, simply click the "X" box on the right. If required, you can also add an output clicking the Add Output button.
Choose a target for each required output — either a new dataset or at an input so that the original image data is modified.
Click the Apply button to process the selected output(s).
After processing is complete, the results will be available in the Data Properties and Settings panel.

documents.title: Frequency Domain Filters
documents.text:
Frequency Domain Filters
Two filters — Discrete Fourier Transform and Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform — are available for transforming time domain signals to the frequency domain and for inverting transformed signals.
The perfect invert-ability of the Discrete Fourier Transform is an important property for building filters which remove noise or particular components of a signals spectrum. Although frequency artifacts can be common in the result of a Fourier transform, these artifacts do not result in error in the inverted signal.
Frequency domain filters
What it does
Discrete Fourier Transform
The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) takes a signal in the so-called time domain (where each sample in the signal is associated with a time) and maps it, without loss of information, into a frequency domain series, where each value is a complex number that is associated with a given frequency. The outputs of the DFT are the magnitude and phase information, as well as the real (even) and imaginary (odd) parts of the transform.
Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform
The Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform (IDFT) takes the frequency series of complex values and maps them back into the original time series. Assuming that the original time series consisted of real values, the result of the IDFT will be complex numbers where the imaginary part is zero. The required inputs of the IDFT are the magnitude and phase information.

documents.title: Image Filtering Window
documents.text:
Image Filtering Window
Image filtering operations are available in the Image Filtering panel, which appears in a contextual window that provides a large display area for creating previews and basic tools for manipulating previews.
Image Filtering contextual window
A. Tools panels B. Image Processing panel C. Views D. Data Properties and Settings panel
Tools Panels
Provides basic tools for synchronizing previews with the original data, manipulating views (see Using the Manipulate Tools), adding annotations (see Annotate Tools), and adjusting window leveling (see Window Leveling) are available on the Tools panels on the left sidebar. Additional options let you select views properties (see 2D Scene's Views Properties) and probe data values (see Using the Probe Tools).
Image Filtering Panel
Controls for applying standard image filters and arithmetic operations to image data are available in the Image Filtering panel, shown below.
Image Filtering panel
A. Operations B. Output
Operations
Provides controls for adding operations to a workflow, selecting inputs and processing settings, and previewing operations on representative dataset slices (see Filtering Images).
Output
Provides options for selecting the required outputs from an image processing workflow and applying operations. Processing operations can be applied by one of two mechanisms — either at the input so that the original image data is modified, or at the output so that a new dataset is created.
Unless you choose to work with the Advanced Options, all inputs in the Image Processing panel must have the same characteristics — size, location, spacing, orientation, and data type — to be used simultaneously in a standard image processing workflow. With the Advanced Options, you can choose inputs with variable sizes, location, and spacing, as well as select different geometries and data types for your image processing outputs (see Working with the Advanced Options).
Views
Allows you to evaluate the effects of applying selected operations at their current settings. Previews can be synchronized with the original data for easy reference.
Data Properties and Settings Panel
Provides access to imported image data and exported outputs (see Image Properties and Settings), as well as tools for evaluating filtering effects, such as line profiles and histograms (see Profiling Intensity and Plotting Histograms from Annotations).

documents.title: Image Filtering
documents.text:
Image Filtering
Image filtering is the term used for any operation, such as smoothing, sharpening, edge enhancement, or thresholding, that is applied to the pixels in an image. Dragonfly provides standard image filters, as well as arithmetic operations to improve image quality. As an alternative, you can process images with trained deep models for denoising and super-resolution (see Training Deep Models for Denoising and Training Deep Models for Super Resolution).
